title: Planet Size Comparison
summary: Line the planets up as spheres at one scale and the size story writes itself: Jupiter is 11 Earths wide and could swallow over 1,300 Earths by volume, Saturn is 9, the ice giants 4, and Mercury is barely half Earth's width. Add the Sun and it dwarfs them all at 109 Earths across.

The Sun added at the same scale
processes: Comparing radii at one consistent scale
How volume grows with the cube of radius
Appreciating the Sun's place in the family
plainLanguageExplanation: If you line up all eight planets next to each other at the same scale, you can finally see the size story that photos hide. Earth sits in the middle of the pack — about 12,700 km across. Mercury, the smallest planet, is barely more than half that. Mars is about half of Earth, Venus almost a twin. Then come the giants: Neptune and Uranus about 4 Earths wide, Saturn 9, and Jupiter a giant 11 Earths wide. Because spheres hold volume by radius cubed, Jupiter doesn't hold 11 times as much 'stuff' as Earth — it holds more than 1,300 times as much. And the Sun makes the whole lineup look small: it is 109 Earths across, so more than a million Earths could fit inside it. This component's model lines the spheres up on a shelf, labels each one in Earths, and has a special toggle that drops little Earth-sized spheres into Jupiter so the volume jump becomes visible.

whyItMatters: Size decides almost everything about a planet — how much material it holds, how strong its gravity is, what its interior pressure is like, and whether it can hold an atmosphere. The radius-to-volume jump also teaches a genuinely important math idea: doubling a sphere's size means eight times the material. When scientists compare exoplanets to Earth, this is the first calculation they make — and it is the same math behind 'one balloon has eight times the air of a half-size balloon.'
tagline: One shelf, one scale, all eight worlds
didYouKnow: If Earth were the size of a marble, Jupiter would be the size of a basketball, and the Sun would be a giant sphere about 11 metres across.
compareReason: This component shows how big the planets are relative to each other; the Scale component shows how far apart the same planets are — size and distance are the two numbers every planet model must get right.
